source: The common practices of maaser kesafim as taught in Modern Orthodox communities, and the United States rules on charitable deductions, donor-advised funds and qualified charitable distributions as of 2026.
confidenceNote: This page does not decide halacha. It shows the arithmetic under each common approach so a family can bring one number to their rav. The tax notes are general and change with the law.

rates.label: A fifth (chomesh)
rates.note: The generous measure, for those who can.

rates.label: Your own share
rates.note: Type the share you have settled on.

bases.label: Income after tax
bases.note: The widely followed view: the tax never reached your hands.

questions: Does my children's tuition count? Most say the basic obligation does not; some allow the part of full tuition that carries another family. Ask.
Is maaser owed on the employer's retirement match, on a gift, on an inheritance, on a tax refund?
May maaser money pay for a family member in need, or for the kiddush I sponsor?
Should the shul's dues come from maaser? Many hold dues are a fee, not tzedakah, but a voluntary gift above the dues is.

tax.label: A donor-advised fund
tax.note: Give appreciated stock in a high-income year, take the deduction then, and grant it out over the years that follow. Useful when a bonus or a sale lands.

tax.label: Appreciated stock
tax.note: Giving shares held over a year skips the capital gains tax and deducts the full value, for a family that itemizes.

tax.label: A qualified charitable distribution
tax.note: From age 70 and a half, money sent straight from an IRA to a charity is not income at all. It counts toward a required distribution.

tax.label: Bunching
tax.note: Two years of giving in one year can lift a family over the standard deduction; the donor-advised fund makes this easy.
